Rooted|1.warmup: Why we warm up: cold muscles and stiff joints lift less and get hurt more. Spend about 7 minutes on this. Do the warm-up movements in order, using only your bodyweight or a very light load, and move through the full range slowly. Then do 2 to 3 ramp-up sets of your first main lift: about 50 percent of your working weight for 5 reps, 70 percent for 3 reps, 85 percent for 1 to 2 reps. The warm-up should leave you feeling warmer, looser and a little more awake, not tired.
Rooted|1.finisher: Cool-down: do not skip this, it helps your body shift out of work mode. Walk slowly for 2 minutes until your breathing returns to normal. Then spend 1 minute stretching the muscles you just trained. Hold each stretch about 30 seconds, breathe slowly, and stop at mild tension, never pain. Finish with 1 minute of 90/90 breathing: lie on your back, knees bent, and breathe into your ribs and belly to let your core and pelvic floor relax.
Rooted|1.notes: Day A: warm up well, then build to your first working set gradually. New to the gym? Here is how to read your workout. A set is a group of reps with a rest after it. RPE is how hard a set feels on a 1 to 10 scale, and RIR means reps in reserve, how many more good reps you could still do. Stopping with 1 to 2 reps in reserve (RPE 8 to 9) is the sweet spot: hard enough to grow, safe enough to keep good form. Choose a weight you could lift 1 to 2 more times with solid form. If you are unsure, start lighter, because it is easy to add weight next time. Form beats weight every time. If your form breaks, stop the set and rest. Rest 2 to 3 minutes between main sets so your muscles are ready to go again. Use the time to sip water and breathe. To progress, once you hit the top of the listed rep range on every set with good form, add the smallest weight increase available (about 2 to 5 pounds) next session. Every fourth week is a deload week: use lighter weights and fewer sets so your body can absorb the work. This is planned, so it does not mean you are slacking. Too hard? Cut the sets by one, lower the weight, or swap to the easier alternate. Too easy? Slow down the lowering phase to 3 seconds before adding weight. What to expect: mild muscle soreness 1 to 2 days later is normal, especially in your first few weeks. Sharp, pinching or joint pain is not. If something hurts in a way that feels wrong, stop that movement and use the alternate in the app. This is general coaching, not medical advice, so check with a doctor first if you have an injury or a health condition. Exhale through the hardest part of each rep, and avoid holding your breath or bearing down. If you notice pelvic heaviness, pressure or leaking, switch to the Pelvic Floor alternate and mention it to a pelvic health physiotherapist. Energy changes across the cycle for some women. See the Cycle Notes tab and adjust effort, not the plan. Arm finisher: the last two exercises (A1 and A2) are a superset, which means you do them back to back with no rest between. Do a set of the curl (A1), go straight into a set of the triceps move (A2), then rest 45 to 60 seconds and repeat for the listed rounds. Biceps and triceps are opposite muscles, so one rests while the other works, which keeps this quick. Use a light to moderate weight and stop each set with 2 to 3 reps still in the tank. Your arms already worked hard on today's presses and rows, so there is no need to chase the burn. Stop and swap the exercise if you feel sharp pain in the elbow.
Rooted|1.purpose: Today's job is to make you stronger. Strength is built by lifting challenging weights with good form, resting properly, and repeating it week after week. This is a full-body day, which means every major area gets trained, so no single session is a make-or-break and you recover well between them. Day A leads with the squat pattern, so your legs get your freshest effort. Pick weights you could lift one or two more times with good form, not weights that make you grind. The goal is steady, repeatable progress, and showing up matters more than any one heavy day. This session is built to take about 45 minutes including the warm-up and cool-down.

Rooted|2.warmup: The easy walk is your warm-up. Keep it at a conversational pace, then move into the core and mobility work at a low effort. Nothing here should feel hard.
Rooted|2.finisher: Finish with 3 minutes of slow breathing. Lie on your back or sit comfortably, breathe in for 4 seconds, out for 6 seconds. This slows your heart rate and helps you recover.
Rooted|2.notes: Everything is done at home with no equipment. Easy effort only. Finish feeling better than you started. If you feel good, resist the urge to turn it into a workout. That is how people stall. Two short core holds are included. Hold each one steady, breathe normally and stop the set before your form slips. Breathe out as you brace, never hold your breath or bear down. If you notice pressure, doming in the belly or leaking, pause and use an easier version.
Rooted|2.purpose: Today's job is to help you recover, not to train. Gentle, easy movement sends blood to sore muscles and loosens stiff joints, which helps you feel better for your next lifting day. Everything today needs no equipment and can be done at home. If you are tempted to push harder, don't. Hard effort today steals energy from the sessions that actually build you. You should finish feeling better than you started. Core work for the whole plan lives on your recovery days on purpose. A strong core protects your back and carries over to every lift, and training it here means it never leaves you tired before heavy sets. This session is built to take 30 minutes or less.
